context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(x \le 3\), draw the line \(x = 3\), which is a vertical line. The origin \((0,0)\) satisfies \(x \le 3\), so the solution set is the origin side of the line, i.e. all points lying on and to the left of the line \(x = 3\). (fig 7.12)

context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(y \ge -2\), draw the line \(y = -2\), which is a horizontal line. The origin \((0,0)\) satisfies \(y \ge -2\), so the solution set is the origin side of the line, i.e. all points lying on and above the line \(y = -2\). (fig 7.13)

context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(x + 2y \le 0\), draw the line \(x = -2y\), which passes through the origin. Points on the line: \((0,0), (-2,1), (-4,2), (2,-1)\). Since the origin lies on the line, choose another test point \((-2,-2)\): \(x + 2y = -2 - 4 = -6 < 0\). Hence the solution set is the half-plane containing the point \((-2,-2)\). (fig 7.14)

context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(2x + 3y \ge 6\), draw the line \(2x + 3y = 6\) through \((3,0)\) and \((0,2)\). Testing the origin: \(2x + 3y|_{(0,0)} = 0 < 6\), so the required region is the non-origin side of the line. (fig 7.15)

context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(2x - 3y \ge -6\), draw the line \(2x - 3y = -6\) through \((-3,0)\) and \((0,2)\). Testing the origin: \(2x - 3y|_{(0,0)} = 0 > -6\), so the required region is the origin side of the line. (fig 7.16)

context: Show the solution sets for the following inequations graphically.
solution: To draw \(4x - 5y \le 20\), draw the line \(4x - 5y = 20\) through \((5,0)\) and \((0,-4)\). Testing the origin: \(4x - 5y|_{(0,0)} = 0 < 20\), so the required region is the origin side of the line. (fig 7.17)

stem: Represent the solution set of the inequation \(3x + 2y \le 6\) graphically.
solution: To draw \(3x + 2y \le 6\), draw the line \(3x + 2y = 6\) through \((2,0)\) and \((0,3)\). Testing the origin: \(3x + 2y|_{(0,0)} = 0 < 6\), so the required region is the origin side of the line. (fig 7.18)

stem: Find the common region of the solutions of the inequations \(x + 2y \ge 4\), \(2x - y \le 6\).
solution: Draw the lines \(x + 2y = 4\) through \((4,0)\) and \((0,2)\), and \(2x - y = 6\) through \((3,0)\) and \((0,-6)\). For \(x + 2y \ge 4\) the region is the non-origin side of its line; for \(2x - y \le 6\) the region is the origin side of its line. The common (overlapping) shaded region is the required solution. (fig 7.19)

stem: Find the graphical solution of \(3x + 4y \le 12\), and \(x - 4y \le 4\).
solution: Draw the lines \(L_1: 3x + 4y = 12\) through \((4,0)\) and \((0,3)\), and \(L_2: x - 4y = 4\) through \((4,0)\) and \((0,-1)\). Testing the origin, both inequations \((\le)\) hold on the origin side of their respective lines. The common shaded region is the graphical solution. (fig 7.20)

stem: Find the graphical solution of the system of inequations \(2x + y \le 10\), \(2x - y \le 2\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\).
solution: Draw \(L_1: 2x + y = 10\) through \((0,10)\) and \((5,0)\); the region \(2x + y \le 10\) is the origin side of \(L_1\). Draw \(L_2: 2x - y = 2\) through \((0,-2)\) and \((1,0)\); the region \(2x - y \le 2\) is the origin side of \(L_2\). Together with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\), the common shaded region OABCO is the graphical (feasible) solution. (fig 7.21)

stem: Find the feasible solution of the system of inequations \(3x + 4y \ge 12\), \(2x + 5y \ge 10\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\).
solution: Draw \(L_1: 3x + 4y = 12\) through \((0,3)\) and \((4,0)\); the region \(3x + 4y \ge 12\) is the non-origin side of \(L_1\). Draw \(L_2: 2x + 5y = 10\) through \((0,2)\) and \((5,0)\); the region \(2x + 5y \ge 10\) is the non-origin side of \(L_2\). Together with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\), the common shaded region is the feasible solution. (fig 7.22)

stem: A manufacturer produces two items A and B. Both are processed on two machines I and II. A needs 2 hours on machine I and 2 hours on machine II. B needs 3 hours on machine I and 1 hour on machine II. If machine I can run maximum 12 hours per day and II for 8 hours per day, construct a problem in the form of inequations and find its feasible solution graphically.
solution: Let \(x\) units of product A and \(y\) units of product B be produced, so \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\). Machine I gives \(2x + 3y \le 12\) and Machine II gives \(2x + y \le 8\). Draw \(L_1: 2x + 3y = 12\) through \((0,4)\) and \((6,0)\); the required region is the origin side of \(L_1\). Draw \(L_2: 2x + y = 8\) through \((0,8)\) and \((4,0)\); the required region is the origin side of \(L_2\). Together with \(x \ge 0\) and \(y \ge 0\), the common shaded region OABCO is the feasible region. (fig 7.23)

A company produces two types of articles A and B which requires silver and gold. Each unit of A requires 3 gm of silver and 1 gm of gold, while each unit of B requires 2 gm of silver and 2 gm of gold. The company has 6 gm of silver and 4 gm of gold. Construct the inequations and find the feasible solution graphically.

A furniture dealer deals in tables and chairs. He has Rs.1,50,000 to invest and a space to store at most 60 pieces. A table costs him Rs.1500 and a chair Rs.750. Construct the inequations and find the feasible solution.
